title-group.article-title: Potential Antidiabetic Effects of Marrubium parviflorum Through Modulation of Oxidative Stress and Hepatoprotection in Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetic Mice

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by persistent hyperglycemia, leading to insulin resistance, β-cell dysfunction, and tissue damage, particularly in the liver. Limitations of conventional antidiabetic therapies have increased interest in medicinal plants with antioxidant and antidiabetic properties. Although several Marrubium species show promising biological effects, evidence for Marrubium parviflorum remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of the methanolic extract of M. parviflorum in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced diabetic mice.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this experimental study, 40 adult male mice were divided into five groups: control, extract control (EXT, 50 mg/kg), STZ-induced diabetic (STZ, 150 mg/kg), STZ + EXT at 50 mg/kg, and STZ + EXT at 100 mg/kg. Treatments were administered orally for 21 days. Blood glucose, serum insulin, oral glucose tolerance test, body weight, and food and water intake were measured. Oxidative stress markers, including malondialdehyde (MDA) and total antioxidant capacity (TAC), as well as serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT) and serum glutamic-pyruvate transaminase (SGPT), were evaluated. Liver histopathology was also assessed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: STZ-induced diabetes increased blood glucose levels (P < 0.001), serum MDA (P < 0.01), SGOT (P < 0.01), and SGPT (P < 0.001), while reducing TAC (P < 0.05) and body weight (P < 0.01) compared with controls. Treatment with EXT significantly reduced blood glucose levels at both 50 and 100 mg/kg (P < 0.05–0.001) and improved glucose tolerance (P < 0.05–0.01). Serum MDA levels were significantly decreased (P < 0.05), whereas TAC was markedly increased at both doses (P < 0.001). SGOT and SGPT levels were significantly reduced at 100 mg/kg (P < 0.05). Histopathological analysis showed improvement in hepatic architecture, with near-normal hepatocyte structure at the higher dose.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: EXT exhibits hypoglycemic, antioxidant, and hepatoprotective effects in diabetic mice, suggesting its potential as a complementary therapeutic for diabetes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Diabetes mellitus is a major global health challenge, affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide and imposing a substantial burden on healthcare systems.1 In 2021, approximately 6.7 million deaths were directly attributable to diabetes, equivalent to one death every 5 seconds. Between 2010 and 2030, the prevalence of diabetes is projected to increase by 69% in developing countries and by 20% in developed countries.2,3 Diabetes is associated with severe complications, including cardiovascular disease, kidney failure, neuropathy, and retinopathy. It is primarily classified into type Ⅰ, caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells, and type Ⅱ, characterized by insulin resistance and β-cell dysfunction. Both types can occur across a wide age range and share overlapping clinical features, highlighting the complexity of disease management.4

Hyperglycemia in diabetes triggers oxidative stress by generating excessive reactive oxygen species, which disrupt cellular signaling pathways and contribute to β-cell dysfunction, insulin resistance, and vascular complications.5 Oxidative stress plays a central role in diabetic complications, and targeting these pathways with antioxidants has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy.6 Despite the availability of conventional therapies such as insulin, metformin, and other oral hypoglycemic agents, achieving optimal glycemic control remains challenging due to side effects, high costs, and poor patient adherence.7 This has stimulated interest in alternative and complementary therapies, particularly herbal medicines, which are rich in bioactive compounds with antioxidant properties that can modulate oxidative stress and improve glucose homeostasis.8

The genus Marrubium (Lamiaceae) comprises approximately 40 species distributed across the Mediterranean region, Europe, and Asia. Several species, including Marrubium vulgare and Marrubium deserti, have demonstrated antidiabetic,9 antioxidant, anti-inflammatory,10 and hepatoprotective effects.11 Marrubium parviflorum, a perennial herb native to Iran, contains flavonoids, phenylethanoid glycosides, phenylpropanoids, and labdane diterpenes, which may contribute to its pharmacological potential.12 Although other Marrubium species have shown hypoglycemic and antioxidant effects in diabetic animal models, limited information exists on the antidiabetic and antioxidant activity of M. parviflorum.9

Various Marrubium species are widely used in gastrointestinal disorders and as anti-inflammatory, antihypertensive, antispasmodic, and antibacterial agents.13 Studies have reported that a hydroalcoholic extract of M. parviflorum aerial parts produced analgesic effects in mice, and aqueous extracts showed the strongest antioxidant activity.14

Other species, such as M. vulgare, exhibit antispasmodic, anticancer, and analgesic effects, largely attributed to their steroid and terpene content and that terpenoid called marrubic acid has been identified in all parts of the M. vulgare plant, associated with antihepatotoxic activity, which is associated with a decrease in serum enzymes such as serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), serum glutamic-pyruvate transaminase (SGPT), and alkaline phosphatase.15 Oral administration of M. vulgare extracts reduced blood glucose and increased plasma insulin in diabetic rats, and M. deserti has shown antioxidant and anti-cholinesterase activities due to its phenolic and flavonoid contents.16

Given the global rise in diabetes, the central role of oxidative stress in its complications, and the promising bioactivity of related Marrubium species, this study aimed to investigate the effects of the methanolic extract of M. parviflorum on glucose regulation, insulin levels, and oxidative stress in diabetic mice.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: Healthy adult male Syrian mice (20–25 g) were obtained from the Pasteur Institute in Tehran, Iran. The animals were housed in standard polypropylene cages and maintained under controlled environmental conditions at 22 ± 2°C and 55 ± 5% relative humidity, with a 12 h light/12 h dark cycle (lights off at 7:00 pm). All animals had free access to standard laboratory chow and water throughout the experimental period. All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with institutional guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals and were approved by the Ethics Committee of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences (ethical approval number: IR.TBZMED.REC.1398.357, approved in 2020).

sec.title: Collection and preparation of M. parviflorum
sec.p: M. parviflorum was processed according to previously reported methods.17 Briefly, the plant was collected in summer from Marand (East Azerbaijan province, Iran) and authenticated by a botanist. The aerial parts were separated, shade-dried at room temperature, and ground into a fine powder using an electric blender. A total of 160 g of the powdered plant material was subjected to sequential solvent extraction using a Soxhlet apparatus: petroleum ether for 36 h, chloroform for 36 h, and methanol for 60 h. The extracts were filtered, concentrated, and dried under reduced pressure at low temperature using a rotary evaporator. The final dried extracts were stored at 4°C until further use. Finally, the extract of 160 g of M. parviflorum plant powder contained 2.151 g of petroleum ether, 1.84 g of chloroform, and 18.2578 g of methanol.

sec.title: M. parviflorum extract (EXT) antioxidant assay
sec.p:
After extraction, a DPPH assay was performed on methanol extracts. DPPH (C18H12N5O6) was used as the free radical.18 First, a 1 mg/mL methanol extract was prepared, sonicated, and homogenized. It was then diluted 7 times, with each dilution reducing the concentration by half (volume = 2 cc). After preparing the different extract concentrations, an 8 mg/100 mL DPPH solution in methanol was prepared. 2 mL of the DPPH solution was added to the test tubes. After 30 min, the absorbance of the new solutions was measured at 518 nm. To prepare a blank solution, 2 cc of DPPH solution was dissolved in 2 cc of methanol. Finally, the absorbance values were adjusted using the equation: (absorbance of the control sample − absorbance of the control sample)/(absorbance of the control sample). The resulting numbers were used to draw a calibration curve and to evaluate IC50, the concentration of the substance of interest that causes a 50% reduction in DPPH free radicals. The IC50 obtained from the DPPH assay of the methanol extract of the plant was 29.74 µg/mL (Figure 1).Figure 1
The RC50 obtained in the DPPH test of the methanol extract was 29.74 µg/mL.Figure 1 dummy alt text

sec.title: Experimental design
sec.p:
Forty male mice were randomly assigned to five groups (n = 8 per group):1.
Saline control group (Cont): received 0.9% saline solution (0.1 mL/day, orally).2.
Extract control group (EXT): received EXT (50 mg/kg/day, gavage).3.
Diabetic group (streptozotocin [STZ]): received a single intraperitoneal (IP) injection of STZ (150 mg/kg) to induce diabetes.4.
STZ + EXT50 group: diabetic mice treated with 50 mg/kg/day of EXT for 21 days after diabetes induction.5.
STZ + EXT100 group: diabetic mice treated with 100 mg/kg/day of EXT for 21 days after diabetes induction.

Mice were individually identified by tail tagging with a nontoxic permanent marker. The procedure was performed gently to minimize stress and handling time and had no adverse effects on animal welfare or physiological parameters. Two days before the sampling surgery, after 9 h of fasting, an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) was performed. After the interventions, the animals were deeply anesthetized, and blood samples were collected to measure serum levels of insulin, malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and SGOT and SGPT. Liver tissue was also isolated for histological evaluation.

sec.title: Diabetes induction
sec.p: To induce diabetes, the treatment and diabetic control groups received a single IP injection of STZ (150 mg/kg), freshly prepared in citrate buffer immediately before administration to prevent decomposition. Five days after STZ injection, fasting blood glucose levels were measured, and mice with glucose concentrations above 200 mg/dL were considered diabetic and included in the study. Animals with lower glucose levels were excluded. Body weight, fasting blood glucose, and food and water intake were monitored before diabetes induction and every 3 days thereafter throughout the experimental period.19

sec.title: Measurement of body weight, food, and water intake variation
sec.p: Body weight was monitored every 3 days. Food intake was determined by measuring the difference between the remaining food and the amount served. Similarly, water intake was measured as the difference between the remaining water and the amount served.

sec.title: Oral glucose tolerance test
sec.p: The OGTT measures the rate of glucose excretion from the body after a 5-h fast. On the 18th day of the experiment, animals were given 2 g/kg of glucose. Blood glucose levels were measured at 0, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min after glucose gavage.

sec.title: Sampling
sec.p: Two days after the OGTT, the animals were deeply anesthetized by IP injection of ketamine (100 mg/kg) and xylazine (10 mg/kg). Blood samples were collected for serum biochemical analysis, and liver tissue was excised for histological evaluation.

sec.title: Assessment of serum glucose and insulin levels
sec.p: Concentrations of plasma glucose and insulin were measured using the Glucose C2 Test Wako Kit (Fujifilm Wako Pure Chemical Co, Osaka, Japan) and the Mouse Insulin ELISA Kit (Caresens), respectively.

sec.title: Assessment of serum SGOT and SGPT levels
sec.p: The activities of hepatic enzymes SGOT and SGPT were determined in plasma samples spectrophotometrically, as described by the manufacturer, using colorimetric commercial kits (Pars Azmoon, Tehran, Iran).

sec.title: Determination of serum MDA and TAC levels
sec.p: MDA, a thiobarbituric acid-reactive substance, was measured as a marker of oxidative stress in serum using the colorimetric method described by Satoh. The lipid peroxide concentration was measured spectrophotometrically at 530 nm.

The ferric acid reducing ability of plasma was used to measure plasma’s TAC. At acidic pH, the ferric tripyridyl triazine complex is reduced to the ferrous state, producing an intense blue color with a maximum absorption at 593 nm. The change in absorbance is proportional to the sample’s antioxidant capacity.

sec.title: Histopathological examination
sec.p: Liver samples fixed in 10% formalin were paraffin-embedded. Blocks were prepared. Sections 5 μm thick were cut and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Microscopic observations were performed to evaluate histological changes. Slides were examined under a light microscope (Model: BX51, Olympus, 400× magnification) and compared with the control.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9.0). Results are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Data were tested for normality using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. A two-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was used to identify significant differences in food and water intake, weight changes, OGTT, and blood glucose among groups. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was used to analyze other parameters of this study. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test was also used to analyze data from H&E staining, liver enzymes, insulin levels, and oxidative stress markers. A P value of less than 0.05 indicated statistical significance.

sec.title: Effect of M. parviflorum extract on food intake, water intake, weight variation, and OGTT test in diabetic mice
sec.p:
Based on a two-way ANOVA of food intake, the day factor did not have a significant effect (F(5, 210)=0.561, P = 0.729), but the group effect was significant (F(4, 210)=13.06, P < 0.0001). Although food intake in the control and EXT groups remained similar and was higher than in the STZ groups, and all STZ-induced diabetic groups had lower food intake than the control group, these differences were not statistically significant. In the STZ + EXT50 group, food intake increased slightly, while in the STZ + EXT100 group, it decreased on average. However, there was no significant days × groups interaction (F(20, 210) = 0.478, P = 0.972) (Figure 2A).Figure 2
The effect of Marrubium parviflorum extract on food intake, water intake, weight variation, and OGTT test in diabetic mice. (A) Food intake on days 4, 7, 7,10, 13, 16, and 19; (B) water intake on days 4, 7, 10, 13, 13,16, and 19; (C) weight variation on days 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, and 19; (D) OGTT test at 0, 30, 60, 90, and 120 min (***P < 0.001 compared to control group; ###P < 0.001, ##P < 0.01, #P < 0.05 compared to STZ group). Data are presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 8).Figure 2 dummy alt text

Regarding water intake, day (F(5, 185)=6.823, P < 0.0001) and group (F(4, 185)=409.3, P < 0.0001) had a significant effect. A significant interaction between days × groups was also observed (F(20, 185)=7.507, P < 0.0001). In multiple comparisons, the STZ group showed a significant increase in water intake across all diabetic groups on all days (P < 0.0001), indicating binge drinking. Water intake remained lower in the control and EXT groups and was not significantly different. Compared with the control group, the STZ group showed a significant increase in water intake throughout the study (P < 0.001). Treatment with EXT50 significantly reduced water intake on days 7 and 10 compared with the STZ group (P < 0.001). However, water intake increased with continued administration. In the diabetic group receiving EXT100, water intake was significantly reduced on days 7 (P < 0.05) and 19 (P < 0.001) (Figure 2B).

Evaluation of the effects of day and group factors on body weight changes revealed a significant effect of day (F(5, 245)=2.348, P = 0.0319) and group (F(4, 245)=34.44, P < 0.0319). A significant interaction between days × groups was also observed (F(24, 245)=1.830, P = 0.0123). In multiple comparisons, body weight increased gradually in both the control and EXT groups throughout the experiment. In contrast, STZ-diabetic rats showed significant weight loss on days 13 (P < 0.01) and 19 (P < 0.001) compared with the control group. The diabetic group receiving 50 mg/kg of the extract also lost weight and differed significantly from the diabetic control group on day 19 (P < 0.05). The STZ + EXT100 group initially lost weight until day 7 and then recovered slightly, resulting in a significant increase in body weight compared with the STZ group on days 16 (P < 0.01) and 19 (P < 0.01) (Figure 2C).

Statistical analysis of the OGTT showed that the minute factor (F(4, 175)=2.853, P = 0.0253) and the group factor had a significant effect (F(4, 175)=89.02, P < 0.0001) on blood glucose levels. The minutes × groups interaction was not significant (F(16, 175)=0.3564, P = 0.9898). In multiple comparisons, blood glucose levels in the control and EXT groups increased for 30 min after glucose administration, then gradually decreased until the end of the experiment. In the STZ group, blood glucose remained significantly higher than in the control group throughout the experiment (P < 0.001). The STZ + EXT50 group significantly reduced blood glucose compared with the STZ group at all time points (30 and 60 min, P < 0.05; 90 and 120 min, P < 0.01). Similarly, the STZ + EXT100 group showed a decrease in blood glucose after peaking at 60 min. This decrease was significant at 90 and 120 min (P < 0.05 and P < 0.01, respectively), and the STZ + EXT100 group had a lower total glucose level than the STZ group (Figure 2D).

sec.title: Effect of M. parviflorum extract on blood glucose levels and serum insulin levels in diabetic mice
sec.p:
Figure 3 shows the blood glucose and serum insulin levels in the experimental groups during the study period. For blood glucose levels, the day factor had no significant effect (F(6, 245)=1.986, P = 0.0682), whereas the group factor showed a significant effect (F(4, 245)=179.0, P < 0.0001). The days × groups interaction was not significant (F(24, 245)=1.069, P = 0.3798).Figure 3
The effect of Marrubium parviflorum extract on blood glucose levels and serum insulin levels in diabetic mice. (A) Blood glucose levels on days 7, 10, 13, 16, and 19. (B) Serum insulin levels (***P < 0.001, *P < 0.05 compared to control group; ###P < 0.001, ##P < 0.01, #P < 0.05 compared to STZ group). Data are presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 8).Figure 3 dummy alt text

The Multiple comparison showed that glucose levels were constant in the control and EXT groups, whereas STZ-induced diabetic rats had higher blood glucose than the control group (P < 0.001). EXT treatment significantly reduced blood glucose levels in diabetic rats. In the STZ + EXT50 group, decreases were observed on days 4 (P < 0.001), 7 (P < 0.001), and 16 (P < 0.05) compared with the STZ group. The higher dose of EXT (100 mg/kg) produced a stronger hypoglycemic effect, with significant reductions on days 4, 7, and 10 (P < 0.001) as well as on days 16 (P < 0.01) and 19 (P < 0.01) (Figure 3A). Serum insulin levels in the diabetic control group were significantly lower than in the control group (1.8160 vs 2.0260 µIU/mL; P < 0.05). Administration of the extract at doses of 50 and 100 mg/kg resulted in increased insulin levels (1.8580 and 1.9060 µIU/mL, respectively) compared with the diabetic control group; however, this increase was not statistically significant (Figure 3B).

sec.title: Effect of M. parviflorum extract on serum SGOT and SGPT levels in diabetic mice
sec.p:
Figure 4 illustrates the effect of the EXT on serum SGOT and SGPT levels in diabetic mice. In the control group, SGOT and SGPT levels were 173 IU/L and 25.67 IU/L, respectively. STZ-induced diabetic mice had significantly higher SGOT (P < 0.01) and SGPT (P < 0.001) than controls. The STX + EXT50 group had lower SGOT and SGPT than the STZ group, but these reductions were not statistically significant. The STZ + EXT100 group significantly reduced both SGOT (P < 0.05) and SGPT (P < 0.05) compared with the STZ group, indicating a hepatoprotective effect of EXT.Figure 4
The effect of Marrubium parviflorum extract on serum SGOT and SGPT levels in diabetic mice. (A) Serum SGOT levels. (B) SGPT levels (***P < 0.001, **P < 0.01 compared to control group; #P < 0.05 compared to STZ group). Data are presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 5).Figure 4 dummy alt text

sec.title: Effect of M. parviflorum extract on serum MDA and TAC levels in diabetic mice
sec.p:
An assessment of the effects of the EXT on serum MDA and TAC in diabetic mice was conducted. STZ-induced diabetes significantly increased serum MDA in the STZ group compared with the control group (P < 0.01). Treatment with the extract in the STZ + EXT50 group significantly reduced MDA (P < 0.05), and the 100 mg/kg dose also significantly decreased it (P < 0.05). Regarding TAC, diabetes induction significantly reduced serum TAC in the STZ group compared with the control group (P < 0.05). Treatment with the extract significantly increased TAC at 50 mg/kg (P < 0.001) and at 100 mg/kg (P < 0.001) (Figure 5).Figure 5
The effect of Marrubium parviflorum extract on serum TAC and MDA levels in diabetic mice. (A) Serum TAC levels. (B) Serum MDA levels (**P < 0.01, *P < 0.05 compared to control group; #P < 0.05, ###P < 0.001 compared to STZ group). Data are presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 5).Figure 5 dummy alt text

sec.title: Effect of M. parviflorum extract on hepatocyte structure in diabetic mice
sec.p:
Histopathological evaluation of liver tissue in experimental groups showed that the control and EXT groups had normal hepatocyte structure. In the diabetic control group (STZ), hepatocytes showed structural abnormalities, including sinus enlargement, inflammation, necrosis, and fat accumulation. Quantification using ImageJ and analysis with one-way ANOVA showed that the percentage of steatosis and necrosis areas was significantly higher than in the control group (P < 0.001). Treatment with EXT improved hepatocyte morphology and liver structure. In the STZ + EXT50 group, the percentage of steatosis areas (P < 0.01) and Necrosis areas (P < 0.001) was significantly reduced, and in the STZ + EXT100 group, the percentage of steatosis areas (P < 0.001) and Necrosis areas (P < 0.001) was significantly reduced compared to the diabetic group (Figure 6).Figure 6
The effect of Marrubium parviflorum extract on hepatocyte structure in diabetic mice. H&E staining. (A) Control group: normal hepatocytes. EXT50 group: normal hepatocytes. STZ group: abnormal hepatocytes, sinus enlargement, inflammation, necrosis, and fat accumulation. STZ + EXT50 group: slight changes in cellular structure and reduced inflammation, necrosis, and fat accumulation. STZ + EXT100 group: regular hepatocyte structure and reduced inflammation, necrosis, and fat accumulation. (B) Percentage of steatosis areas (***P < 0.001 compared to control group; ##P < 0.01 and ###P < 0.001 compared to STZ group). (C) percentage of necrosis areas (***P < 0.001 compared to control group; ###P < 0.001 compared to STZ group. Data are presented as the mean ± SEM (n = 3).Figure 6 dummy alt text

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Given the increasing global prevalence of diabetes mellitus, growing interest in herbal medicines for diabetes management, and limited data on the antidiabetic potential of M. parviflorum, the present study was designed to evaluate the effects of M. parviflorum methanolic extract on metabolic, oxidative, and hepatic biomarkers in STZ-induced diabetic mice. STZ induces insulin-dependent diabetes primarily by selectively destroying pancreatic β-cells, mediated by cellular uptake via the GLUT2 transporter, followed by DNA alkylation and oxidative damage.20 Previous studies have reported antidiabetic effects of various Marrubium species.21,22 supporting the rationale for investigating M. parviflorum.

In the current study, IP administration of M. parviflorum extract (50 and 100 mg/kg) for 21 days reduced blood glucose levels in diabetic mice, with the higher dose producing a more pronounced hypoglycemic effect. This effect may be attributed to the extract’s protective action against STZ-induced β-cell damage or to enhanced insulin sensitivity and peripheral glucose utilization. Although serum insulin levels increased modestly in extract-treated groups, the changes were not statistically significant, suggesting that the glucose-lowering effects may occur predominantly through insulin-independent mechanisms.

Diabetic mice exhibited significant weight loss, consistent with enhanced catabolic processes, including lipolysis and proteolysis, under insulin-deficient conditions. Similar findings have been reported in STZ-induced diabetic models.23,24 Notably, treatment with 100 mg/kg of M. parviflorum extract led to a significant recovery in body weight by day 19, indicating partial restoration of metabolic balance.

The OGTT further demonstrated improved glucose handling in extract-treated diabetic mice. This improvement may reflect enhanced insulin action, increased glucose uptake in peripheral tissues, or reduced hepatic glucose output.25 Despite improved glucose tolerance, the lack of a significant increase in insulin levels suggests that M. parviflorum may exert its effects by modulating insulin sensitivity rather than by directly stimulating insulin secretion.

Oxidative stress plays a central role in the pathogenesis of diabetes and its complications.26 Previous studies have confirmed the antioxidant properties of M. parviflorum.27,28 Consistent with these reports, STZ-induced diabetes significantly increased serum MDA levels and reduced TAC, reflecting elevated lipid peroxidation and impaired antioxidant defense.29 Treatment with M. parviflorum extract significantly decreased MDA levels and increased TAC, confirming its potent antioxidant activity, as supported by the DPPH assay results.

Food intake was reduced in diabetic groups compared with healthy controls, indicating diabetes-associated anorexia.30 Administration of the extract did not significantly alter food intake. As expected, diabetic mice exhibited marked polydipsia. Although extract administration initially reduced water intake, prolonged treatment was associated with increased water intake, an unexpected finding that warrants further investigation to clarify the underlying mechanisms.

Hyperglycemia-induced liver damage is commonly associated with elevated serum levels of hepatic enzymes, including SGOT and SGPT.31 In the present study, STZ-induced diabetes significantly increased these enzymes, whereas EXT treatment, particularly at 100 mg/kg, significantly reduced their levels. Histopathological analysis further supported these findings, revealing improved hepatic architecture, reduced sinusoidal dilation, and decreased central vein congestion in extract-treated groups. These observations indicate a hepatoprotective effect of EXT, consistent with previous reports demonstrating the hepatoprotective properties of Marrubium species, including M. vulgare, which has been shown to reduce SGOT, SGPT, and alkaline phosphatase levels.32

Overall, the findings of this study indicate that M. parviflorum exerts antidiabetic, antioxidant, and hepatoprotective effects in STZ-induced diabetic mice, highlighting its potential as a complementary therapeutic for diabetes management.

Limitations of this study include the short treatment duration (3 weeks), the use of a single animal model (STZ-induced diabetes in male mice), and the lack of direct molecular analysis of the signaling pathways involved. Future studies should investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of EXT, including the involvement of specific signaling pathways such as AMPK, PI3K/Akt, GLUT4 translocation, and Nrf2-mediated antioxidant response. Long-term studies in multiple animal models, as well as clinical trials, are warranted to confirm efficacy, safety, and optimal dosing in humans.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study indicated that the methanolic extract of M. parviflorum reduced hyperglycemia, improved antioxidant status, and protected liver tissue in STZ-induced diabetic rats. These effects are likely mediated by modulation of oxidative stress and related metabolic pathways, indicating the potential of this plant as a complementary agent in diabetes management.
